This style was derived from intuitions in linear logic and Lambert calculus, but achieved a significant breakthrough by separating the proof of an statement into two distinct yet equal parts. This research expands upon yinyang proofs and presents a new framework that enables the creation of yinyang proofs for a broader range of statements. Additionally, we show that our method, based on favourite translation, can implicitly derive yinyang proofs for a certain class of statements that involve disjunction and conjunction. We further examine the relationship between yinyang proofs and favourite translation and view the combinatorial yinyang proof style as an innovative way to present proofs that were previously considered difficult to separate into distinct parts. This presentation highlights the potential of yinyang proofs to inspire the creation of new and innovative proof styles. Lastly, we present several examples of yinyang proofs for various types of statements and their negations, demonstrating the versatility and applicability of this style to multiple areas of mathematics and logic.   policies that are easily transferable to new agents. This new direction in

  abstraction in both natural and artificial intelligence. As such, it holds the 
  potential to revolutionize the interface between human and machine intelligence.

  incorporating interpretable human concepts directly into the agent's reward 
  function. Additionally, we outline promising avenues for investigating the

  concept mapping to existing AI frameworks. These extensions and potential 
  applications will be thoroughly discussed in the supplementary material.

Meanwhile, lower frequency fluctuations also show an inverse distance relationship, but its magnitude can't be fully explained by thermal properties alone and indicates that information is being transmitted.  Two possible mechanisms explain this transmission: the way heaters of different sizes respond to changes in temperature and the collective movement of particles under the influence of thermal motion. As the study matches key characteristics of studies on Brownian movement in nature, it suggests that similar mechanisms could be at work in real-life physical processes.  By extending this idea, researchers also discovered how these mechanisms break down when considering fluctuations between the two heat channels, and the potential for this breakdown to facilitate learning and adaptive processes in systems, potentially leading to new discoveries in both technology and biology. Our findings indicate that the model successfully forecasts future infection counts and identifies the prominent age group driving the spread of the disease. In addition, we discuss how the estimated age-specific transmission probabilities and the unique model can be utilized in Age-specific vaccination and policy strategies to combat the outbreak. This model also serves as a foundation for addressing key questions such as how different age groups impact the rapid spread of the disease and how a vaccinated population affects multiple age groups. Yet little is known about the potential for GAN-generated content in forensic science. Our study takes initial steps in this area by examining the capabilities of GANs in creating realistic heads and hands. We utilize two distinct approaches to GANs, Progressive GAN and StyleGAN, and evaluate their performance using quantitative and qualitative assessments. Our results indicate that StyleGAN, although producing images with a different aspect focus, fails to match the accuracy of Progressive GAN. Additionally, our findings suggest that GAN-generated content may not seamlessly integrate into existing databases of biometric data, providing valuable insights for researchers. Our accessible code and synthetic data are available at our GitHub repository: https://github.com/RGULab/GAN-Content-Forensic-Applications. Our synthetic data can also be leveraged in RGULab's BiID, a large, open-source dataset for various computer vision tasks, including novel applications for biometric forensics. This dataset can be found at: https://github.com/RGULab/BiID. Our contribution represents the beginning of exploring GAN-generated content in the realm of forensic science, and we anticipate this line of research to continue yielding valuable insights and practical tools for the field. The ultimate aim is to utilize these tools to raise awareness and simplify the detection of existing biometric surveillance. The study utilizes a matrix-exponential method, inspired by a novel technique previously developed, to achieve highly accurate time-step independent simulations. The results of this research reveal that simple artificial cells incorporating basic mechanisms are capable of generating a range of rhythmic behaviors, including hyperactive and passive states, as well as rhythmic patterns. The association process in JPDA involves combining data on individual objects to create state estimates. Unfortunately, the scalarization process required to integrate velocity and position states constrains the representation of object features, limiting the accuracy of object association and state estimation, particularly in scenarios with noisy data or overlapping object signatures. This investigation is part of our ongoing research aimed at categorizing all Harish-Chandra pairs for the general linear group, which will be detailed in our forthcoming paper. Building on Flath's method for calculating $\xi$, we developed a comparable approach based on the properties of Gallager vectors to determine $a$. We have demonstrated that for a given Gallager vector $g$, its corresponding $a$ can be computed through a permutation dependent on $g$'s entries and its Galois image, which we represent as $\sigma_g$. Furthermore, in cases where $g$ and its Galois image are identical, the resulting $a$ is actually an integer. As cycle representations are more intuitive than Galois images, the correspondence between Harish-Chandra pairs and $p'$-weight cycles becomes a preferable choice. We have found that for a general linear group's Galois image, its $p'$-weight cycles directly correspond to its characteristic polynomials, which in turn relate to the eigenmatrices $\Phi_n$. As an result, properties applicable to these eigenmatrices provide valuable insights into the desired cycle representations. To fill a knowledge gap regarding eigenmatrices, we introduced a new collection called the Eigenmatrix Database (EDB). As of now, the EDB contains over 600,000 uniquely indexed eigenmatrices, which have been carefully evaluated to ensure their accuracy and validity. Although the EDB's current collection represents just a small fraction of the total number of eigenmatrices, it serves as an effective starting point for our research. We have used various computer programs, such as those for the groups $GL_2$ and $GL_3$, to visualize properties like cycle lengths, trace distributions, and eigen eigenvalues distribution, which in turn identified the characteristics of the EDB. In addition, those programs revealed the possibility of representing the Weyl group of $GL_n(q)$ as a forest of trees, which in turn provides the required cycle representations of the Galois images of $\Phi_n(q)$. This discovery has significantly aided our research and offers a new approach for studying the properties of Galois images. Despite the advancements in creating AI systems that explain their decisions, little research has been done on grasping the fundamental learning process of these models. In order to bridge this knowledge gap, we present DdynC, a novel dynamic graph representation for modeling the short-term dynamics of neural network optimization. Specifically, we examine a robust version of the Frequent Elements problem, where a certain number of the most recent elements in the stream must appear more frequently than half of the letters in a fixed string. An adversary aims to prevent the streaming algorithm from accurately processing the stream for a prolonged period. An earlier information-theoretic lower bound by Gupta et al. in TCS 2022 established the minimum frequency count of $\Omega(\sqrt{m}/c^2)$, where $m$ is the string length and $c$ is the string character count. In this work, we create an algorithm, which uses only $O(\log m)$ space and processes the stream in $T$ time, to identify whether the frequent elements occur more than $c$ times within a window of size $T$, with an updated count of $\Omega(m^{1/2} - \log^{3/2} m)$.

reminds you of home, it's a project that uses the principles of fractals to create a visually engaging representation of wireless communication networks. The pattern you see is a result of applying an inverse gamma distribution, specifically $\gamma_x^{-2}$, to the coverage area of each transmitter $x$. In this case, we're looking at $x$ as individual transmitters within a network, and the effect is a beautiful self-similar design. 

This note examines the relationship between the support of this fractal, denoted by $S_\gamma$, and measures of gamma distributions, dendenoted by $f_{\gamma_i}(x)$, as we explore the properties of this intricate fractal. In particular, we define the dimension of this fractal, denoted by $h_\gamma$, in terms of the measure of $S_\gamma$, and express it through the combination of measures of individual $f_{\gamma_i}(x)$. 

Furthermore, our investigation of this fractal extends to its applicability in visual representations of wireless networks, and accordingly, we introduce a set of definitions tailored to capture the essence of this fractal. Additionally, a fast algorithm has been devised to generate this fractal, and the algorithm can also be utilized for creation of custom fractals based on user-specified probability distributions. 

Lastly, in a departure from traditional fractional dimensions discussed in the field, we seek a new definition: the information dimension of networks and signals exhibiting fractal properties, and we propose a specific candidate that involves the measure of individual signals. This new definition is envisioned to foster future research in the area of signal processing and communication, and the potential existence of networks possessing positive measure while possessing a zero classical dimension. 

The research presented here was initiated when the second author, R.R. N. Iyengar, met Professor Grigoryfs at the University of Arizona. Certain established type systems are incapable of accommodating the effects of non-deterministic programming pathways on the typing of programs, primarily due to predictive constraints introduced by polymorphic type features that facilitate composable high-order programming. In response, several recent approaches have relied on trustworthiness as a non-classical form of integrity, requiring that well-typed programs behave as if integrity were guaranteed, which can be dynamically enforced. their authentic nature is often uncertain, raising concerns among audiences due to potential manipulation of their perceptions through malicious alteration of digital content, especially images.  To alleviate these concerns, establishing the original, unaltered version of a digital asset can serve as significant proof.  Although verification techniques exist for certain types of digital content, the process is particularly complex for images due to their high dimensionality and the numerous available transformation techniques.  This study investigates the application of diffusion models to create an innovative solution for detecting an image's authenticity and accurately reconstructing its original state by utilizing a large dataset of edited images and authentic pairs, thereby setting a new record on both accuracy and loss reduction among leading image reconstruction models.  Additionally, the corresponding code and model weights can be accessed via the designated GitHub link.  Our research also illustrates through visualizations that the accuracy of an image reconstruction model serves as an effective counterfeit filter, and we observed less noise in the results when using this approach compared to other methods, indicating improved underlying image reconstruction.  Our study also explored two critical aspects: the stability of the reconstruction model when exposed to a wide range of edited images, and the potential for improving an image reconstruction model by leveraging another model that specializes in a different area, such as image editing.  Through our experiments using a dataset of significantly small sample size, the results indicated that the performance improved when either the original or the transformed image was provided, and the results remained stable even with as few as 5 samples, but the results declined for even lower sample counts.  Finally, the related study found that the initial, unconditional diffusion models performed better as a counterfeit filter compared to their conditional counterparts, and our research also showed that the quality of the transformed image played a critical role in the accuracy of the counterfeit filter, with lower FID scores yielding improved results.  These findings may open up new avenues for improving the performance of digital content detection models in the future.  Our research also highlights the potential for further advancing the state-of-the-art by leveraging additional, real-world instance data in the training of the model, an aspect that is currently being explored in our ongoing research.  Our research also showed that the conditional variant, which produces images based on random noise, cannot be utilized for detecting instances that are similar to one another, an aspect that is also being explored in our ongoing research due to the potential for improving the model's performance using techniques such as metric learning and instance normalization.  Our results also motivated new research directions, including the exploration of unsupervised image reconstruction methods

These dictionaries, generally consisting of simple visual symbols like arrows and shapes, serve as a universal reference to decode the intentions of ambiguous objects. By incorporating such dictionaries, researchers have enjoyed substantial gains in robustness. However, this advantage is fully realized only when dictionaries are treated as entirely separate entities during training, rendering their interactive co-utilization unexplored. Given that real-world objects often blend together, it is essential to develop techniques enabling objects to blend as well. Building upon our previous research, our method has been successfully applied to the issue of named entity recognition, upon which we have also achieved significant improvements in performance. This research extends the existing literature on the long time behavior of the Fokker-Planck equation in several ways. First, it establishes uniqueness of the long time solution for a class of dissipative PDEs in a low regularity space. Second, it provides a regularity result for the long time solution by analyzing the behavior of the solution's gradient. Finally, it provides a complete description of the long time behavior, showing that the solution converges to a equilibrium as time approaches infinity. This research also offers a dynamic description of the long time behavior, showing that the solution's behavior is determined by a specific ordinary differential equation. Ultimately, it provides a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of a global attractor in a low regularity space. This research is particularly notable because the Poincaré-Landau force it incorporates is a key component of the Ginzburg-Landau model for a superfluid. As a result, the findings of this research are highly relevant to the study of pattern formation in the Ginzburg-Landau system. This research builds upon two key papers, one by Briccolini-Mora-Vismara and another by Chueshov-Lu-Strothotte. It uses similar techniques to extend the results of the referenced papers, however, it overcomes the challenge of a nonsmooth perturbation to prove the existence of a global attractor in a low regularity space. As a result, the findings of this research offer significant improvements over the references. Given the inherent limitations of electric vehicle batteries, prohibiting overcharging, we develop a charging schedule with the capability to factor in the level of deterioration, an element traditionally left unaccounted for in prior studies. Additionally, our model incorporates the effect of time-based retention, an aspect not previously explored in the literature. By applying a timing-based retention factor, which undergoes periodic re-evaluation every 'h' time units, our proposed charging schedule is capable of adapting and remains applicable even in scenarios where the retention factor's specific values are unknown at the outset. Experimental results obtained from a comprehensive approach validate the validity and efficacy of the proposed scheduling method. We initially establish a range of retention function possibilities and discover that a linear relationship, represented by the 'r' retention factor, yields substantial improvements of up to 30% in charging efficiency in the majority of examined scenarios. Moreover, our paper delves into the independent contribution of 'r' and 'h' in our proposed charging schedule, enabling the identification of optimal 'r' ranges for various periods of time and revealing a direct relationship between 'h' and charging efficiency. Notably, our proposed charging schedule is demonstrated to be superior to priority-based and pre-existing observation-based approaches in a wide range of actual and synthetic datasets. Since actual EV battery data, a requirement for our proposed charging schedule model, can be costly and time-consuming to obtain, particularly in large quantities, we propose an alternative approach: creating a dataset of critical battery parameters from the seven largest EV manufacturers directly, making it easier to obtain a starting point for implementing our proposed charging schedule. We used the data to run our proposed scheduling method on a real-world dataset and observed a 20.69% increase in charging efficiency. We acknowledge the inherent limitations of 'r' variability and suggest potential avenues for expanding the scope of our proposed charging schedule using reinforcement learning, while also outlining the relevant characteristics of battery capacity and age to enable an enhanced scheduling method with respect to battery degradation in the future. Finally, our proposed idea involves a topological mapping of battery capacity and age characteristics which holds promise for developing a more comprehensive charging schedule model. This mapping could also be useful for creating expert systems that take into account battery age and capacity, thereby providing advice on optimal charging strategies and improving the efficiency of existing EV charging schedules. Our analysis relies on dynamic systems theory, specifically three distinct models, to account for metallicity variations through three distinct phases of galaxy development.  By applying each model to available data on how the mass of stars $M_{\rm star}$, the metallicity $Z$, and other factors changed over time, we calculate the time it takes for the Milky Way to reach its current level of star mass $M_{\rm star} = 0.65 L_{\rm Sun}$ and star metallicity $Z = 0.00184$.  Our results indicate that, based on the most comprehensive data set from the GALFORM model, the galaxy is expected to be fully developed in about 8.7 billion years and, in turn, reach its metallicity peak about 1.1-1.6 billion years later.  Furthermore, this metallicity peak is forecasted to occur within the disk and bulge regions of the galaxy.  Our examination of how the metallicity changes over time in the disk, bulge, and halo regions of the galaxy reveals that, based on the disk model, the galaxy is expected to be fully developed in about 8.7 billion years and, in turn, reach its metallicity peak about 1.6-2.4 billion years later.  Conversely, it may be possible to utilize detailed elements from the age of 12,000,000,000 years to differentiate between distinct galaxy development theories and, in turn, gain a more in-depth understanding of the developmental stages of the galaxy and its underlying metallicity changes over time. of medical data sources and domains, deep learning model applications in medicine are often highly domain-specific due to differences in clinical populations, imaging data, and clinical measurements.  Although deep learning models show impressive in-group predictive abilities, their cross-domain applicability is a major concern, driven by the desire to prevent expensive and time-consuming data collection.  A key related issue is feature representation - what underlying characteristics of medical data can effectively be used for cross-domain prediction?  We investigated this question through a large-scale survey of over 360 medical publications revealing that tabular data, including clinical metadata, may contain useful information for cross-domain transfer learning.  By demonstrating the use of such information in transferring learning from electronic health records to clinical NLP tasks, we highlight its significance and show the potential to overcome the challenges of developing deep learning models for multiple domains.  Our study provides essential knowledge for harnessing the power of meta-data and data annotation to address the complex problem of domain transfer in medicine.  Furthermore, it serves as a foundation for exploring the use of metadata in future medical machine learning systems.  As the adoption of electronic health records continues to grow, the underlying metadata can power more general and effective medical machine learning systems, leading to improved population-level forecasting and decision-making. To address this challenge, we study how to efficiently utilize machine learning for event identification with wearable sensors, a key task in this application area. We implement and evaluate different machine learning techniques, including decision trees and random forests, for classifying events from wearable accelerometers during strenuous physical activities. Given the vast amounts of data involved, we explore how to effectively classify new data points using large existing datasets, also experimenting with various data sampling methods to accelerate the process. Despite the size of the data sets, our research finds that random forest performance peaks at around 90% of original dataset size, and that complex algorithms are outperformed by simpler versions, and these models are consistently superseded by a straightforward approach to event identification. While using existing data for classification is more complicated than initially expected, our experiments show that simple methods consistently outperform more complex ones, and the'most similar neighbors' method excels among them. As random forests perform well on large data sets, we investigate how to efficiently utilize them for new data classification. We compare several strategies to classify new data points, and our analysis reveals that early stopping is often the best approach, as the error rate stops improving beyond a certain number of training samples, also near 90% of the total number. To accelerate the process, we study different methods for selecting representative subsets of data, and our experiments show that using consecutive samples for training is the simplest and most effective strategy. To summarize, our research identifies several opportunities for improving machine learning-based event recognition with wearable sensors: applying simpler algorithms, developing more efficient methods for classifying new data, and exploiting parallel processing capabilities, particularly using the'most similar neighbors' method which doesn't need training.

Because emojis represent a visual representation of meaning, they provide valuable insights into the reviewer's emotional state during the review process, potentially influencing the perceived rating of the product. , there's a growing need for high-capacity optical networks, especially in short-haul systems with low attenuation.  However, the available spectrum in the traditional wavelength-division multiplexing (WDM) system is limited by the E-band, particularly after the elimination of the E1 pulse, leaving us with a shortage of resources.  This problem can be overcome by introducing the E-EXWDM technology, which expands the spectrum into the E-band and enables a larger number of subchannels to be implemented within it.  By using a combination of advanced technologies such as polarisation-identified multiplexing (PIM), equalization (E-QAM), and equal-power allocation (E-PA), the performance of the E-EXWDM system can be optimized, thereby enabling higher data rates in next-generation optical networks. This paper looks at both the benefits and drawbacks of the E-EXWDM system and discusses different design approaches to achieve maximum performance. and theoretically the system of excitons in a bilayer of two-dimensional indium adatom chains on the cleaved surface of boron nitride. The excitons show strong coupling with a neighboring charge carrier, which is a property unique among one-dimensional nanoscale materials. Our investigation reveals the exciton's absorption profile, energy levels, and electronic configuration. Moreover, in combination with the exciton's strong spin-orbit interaction, we observe a specific pattern of exciton absorption near their energy transition, which leads to the formation and measurement of two new energy levels resulting from the interaction between the excitons and spin-orbit influence. This has enabled us to determine the strength of the spin-orbit effect and the spatial arrangement of electronic bonds within the nanochains, which is crucial for their function and stability as quantum devices. Finally, to achieve controllable device functions necessitate the independent control of the excitons and spin properties, which presents significant challenges given the exciton's tendency to transfer energy to nearby excitons, ultimately leading to the formation of bound pairs of excitons. Nonetheless, in this study, we successfully create and manipulate a solitary exciton within the chain, which demonstrates the feasibility of generating and controlling the fundamental units of excitonic matter in the form of singlet excitons. Our innovative approach to designing quantum devices centered around excitons holds potential for the production of quantum light, particularly in the form of entangled photons, which is our main topic of discussion in the conclusion section.  In the conclusion section, we propose an alternative method of creating entangled light using a specific type of exciton interaction known as intervalley scattering. Specifically, we investigate the possibility of generating entangled light through the interaction of excitons within the context of a specific property known as valleytronics, in which electrons switch valleys, resulting in the formation and measurement of highly entangled photons consisting of two energy components, which is a requirement for valleytronics as a quantum technology. Our proposed method of creating entangled light relies on the use of adjacent excitons transferring their energy to each other in a specific pattern, which is a characteristic property of excitons in 2D materials, and presents an ideal solution for generating key resources required for quantum information processing, specifically in the context of valleytronics, which is an emerging field crucial for the development of novel two-dimensional nanoelectronics and nanophotonics based on the concept of valleys. Our suggested protocol could also serve as an energy-efficient alternative to current standard methods used to generate entangled light

Unlocked transmitters pose significant interference to adjacent channels, but can be mitigated through a simple, low-power method - pulse position modulation (PPM). With the aid of our analysis and simulations involving both theoretical models and widely-used sub-THz transmitters from Sigmaлід technology, this paper provides the first comprehensive study of the performance of mmWave/sub-THz base stations in the presence of PPM-modulated transmitter noise. Our research reveals that PPM can be tailored to provide effective interference protection during high-frequency transmission. While PPM might seem to reduce system efficiency, our results show otherwise. In a 60 GHz spectrum, our PPM scheme outperformed traditional methods, with improved throughput in all scenarios and reduced power consumption of around 60%. Notably, our PPM approach enhanced capacity by up to 300% when used in conjunction with optimization techniques involving power management and allocation. As such, this research makes the case for using PPM to protect adjacent frequency bands and promises improved performance in hybrid PPM-modulated transmitter noise scenarios. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the significant performance gains achieved represent a conservative estimate of the potential benefits of PPM usage in sub-THz transmission systems. With further optimization, PPM could potentially add substantial value to existing spectrum usage practices. Our analysis also identified an overlap between PPM and existing techniques like OFDMA in terms of their ability to provide bandwidth division and/or power management, thereby suggesting the potential for PPM to improve the performance of existing spectrum usage scheduling methods when applied to PPM-modulated transmitter noise, leading to a greater good in terms of providing performance and achieving fairness in time-sensitive applications. As such, this research aims to lay the groundwork for future research into the potential benefits of using PPM in schedule-independent scheduling methods, including PPM modulation. This research also aims to serve as a starting point for evaluating the potential consequences of implementing PPM in transmitter noise, including PPM modulation. This is accompanied by numerous concrete examples, illustrations and also potential research directions to enhance the accuracy and applicability of these models in the future. In particular, we believe that enhanced understanding of machine learning-based turbulence models' ability to grasp the underlying turbulent physics will lead to significant advancements in the field. In addition, we outline some open questions and the perspectives of a researcher with over 20 years of experience in the turbulence modeling field. In contrast to previous reviews on Reynolds number and uncertainty in turbulence modeling, here we focus more on the general state of the field and provide specific insights, with less emphasis on the numerical aspects. This is a comprehensive work on the constraints of using ML algorithms for turbulence modeling, with over 130 citations and covering a period of more than 8 years, thus making it a comprehensive works on the subject. In particular, we believe that machine learning-based turbulence models will become a reliable and indispensable tool in both engineering and scientific research. Moreover, we establish a direct relationship between a poset's partition width and width of its linear extension partition width, proving that a poset's partition width is less than $n$ if and only if the width of each of its linear extension partition widths is less than $n$. Furthermore, our work reveals that a uniform poset has a unique partition value if and only if it is atomic or dual atomic, and supports a conjecture proposed by Kim, Kim, and Urrutia as a special case. Finally, our work demonstrates that a uniform poset has inclusive pairings if and only if its distance two diameter is less than or equal to 4, and identifies all uniform posets with a distance two diameter of 4 whose partition values are distinct. technology has the potential to revolutionize the integration of vehicles in smart power grids, with the capability of functioning as both energy consumers and producers during grid-related operations. Despite existing standards for integrating conventional vehicles into power grids, there remains a knowledge gap regarding the standardization of vehicle-to-grid communication. This paper provides an in-depth analysis of the standardization of vehicle-to-grid communication within the context of plug-in electric vehicles, with a focus on their interaction with smart power grids. It delves into the underlying motivations for and challenges associated with this technology, as well as key aspects influenced by mobile network connectivity, vehicle management systems, and power grid management systems. Finally, this paper outlines research directions and proposed future research areas, including the development of vehicle management systems based on grid frequency and vehicle-to-grid communication within mobile networks. The results of this research can serve as a reference for future similar investigations. The research was conducted using a combination of academic studies, industry expert interviews, and standardization organization observations. Moreover, this paper provides an overview of existing and planned standards for vehicle-to-grid communication within the boundaries of current standards, with an assessment of their completeness and potential areas requiring further standardization. Various publicly available open-source vehicle-to-grid communication interfaces were also analyzed to identify existing gaps in standardization requirements. A potential application of our work involves using spin systems to model complex chaotic systems and study their time evolution. Our research may ultimately contribute to a broader understanding of multi-particle systems in chaotic environments, where a single particle's behavior is difficult to predict. This difficulty stems from the challenging nature of modeling these systems when they are in a state of rapid change. Despite existing mathematical theories, such systems prove to be computationally difficult to simulate on typical computers. As a result, researchers have made little progress in developing detailed computational models that accurately capture the spatial patterns and temporal evolution of complex systems throughout their life cycle. This paper presents a new approach for modeling these systems by utilizing deep neural networks to learn their behavior through a technique called backtracking in time. This innovative method allows the reconstruction of a system's earlier states given its current configuration. We demonstrate this approach using the complex phenomenon of pattern formation in soft elastic sheets induced by chemical reactions. Our results show the reconstruction of the system's pattern at a previous time from its pattern at a later time. This technique has the potential to be applied to various other systems including biological and geophysical systems, and could be used to create generative models that produce realistic patterns for systems that progress in a continuous and smooth manner. This model can also be used for a new approach to pattern forecasting by leveraging the system's past states to make more accurate predictions about its future behavior.

Our results show the ability to forecast the location and time of chemical waves in the system.

This has motivated numerous studies aimed at setting lower limits on the primordial black hole mass using various astrophysical data, such as star formation and gravitational lensing effects in galaxies.  Theoretical models of galaxy and star formation often rely on simplified, non-radiative simulations.  Our study incorporates primordial black holes into existing galaxy evolution simulations and produces the first comprehensive numerical bounds on their mass.  Primordial black holes significantly influence galaxy mass distribution within the universe, and significantly influence smaller galaxy masses and their associated star formation rates.  Our results indicate that primordial black holes put a substantial lower bound, near $4.2 \times 10^{5} M_{\odot}$, on their characteristic mass at $z=0$ for galaxies up to $10^{9} M_{\odot}$ in mass.  This new constraint has the potential to rule out vast regions of the cosmic inflation parameter space.  Future research such as Gaia, PLATO, and JWST can verify our findings and supplement current constraints on primordial black holes.  Moreover, the impact of primordial black holes on galaxy evolution is a largely unexplored area of study that merits further research.  Galaxies with irregular mass distributions may be more resistant to the effects of primordial black holes, resulting in a reduced lower bound, while those resistant to feedback may instead experience increased star formation due to the significant impact of primordial black holes on gas within the universe, and predictably higher star formation rates in subsequent generations.  This theoretical framework offers a possible, non-inflating explanation for the missing dark matter within the universe, and presents opportunities for future observational studies to verify these new astrophysical constraints.  This possible explanation for dark matter is distinct from the, currently more popular, scenario in which primordial black holes generate the missing mass through a massive, universe-scale mechanism. Utilizing the Landau free energy expansion from the Helfand-Zhang equation, our analysis shows that the compressibility and specific heat are notably influenced by the pseudospin, leading to differences of up to 100% and 40%, respectively, from their spin-polarized counterparts for Xe-like gases. These variations become less pronounced in other gases such as Rb and 4He-like. Our findings are highly relevant to the current experimental pursuit of creating pure Fermi gases with pseudospin polarized states. The potential application of our work extends to the advancement of our understanding of the specific heat in fermionic systems, including the specific heat contribution from spin-fluctuation in ultracold spinor Fermi gases. This could lead to the development of a novel technique for measuring the Landau constant within the pseudospin framework. Furthermore, our research shows that the specific heat in a pseudospin state is significantly less than in a spin state, indicating the existence of a "specific heat gap" caused by pseudospin polarization. In this study, we tackle two principal difficulties associated with multicasting in EH-driven wireless power transfer (WPT) communication systems, specifically the constraints imposed by power limitations and unreliable energy sources. To address these challenges, we propose an innovative solution involving a base station capable of multicasting, capable of collecting energy, collecting data, transmitting energy, and broadcasting information. We aim to maximize the base station's data transmission rate while maintaining the minimum data rate for each user in each communication time slot. To solve this problem efficiently, we first simplify the complex expression representing the base station's overall energy collection time into a more manageable expression as a function of the number of users. We then utilize this expression to reframe the problem of maximizing the base station's overall transmission rate, first simplifying it through variable substitution, and then leveraging convex optimization techniques to derive an optimal, though approximate, solution for up to 20 users. We also introduce a more efficient suboptimal solution for larger user populations. Our results suggest that our proposed solution significantly outperforms a more traditional approach that does not account for the base station's overall transmission rate. We compare these results with those derived from a more optimal, though computationally intensive, method and verify that the proposed solution achieves a within 0.1-bit/second information rate loss. For larger user populations, our proposed solution exhibits only a within 0.05-bit/second information rate loss when compared to the optimal solution. We recognize that the derived suboptimal solution may experience a performance degradation when confronted with an increasingly larger number of users. To overcome this limitation, we propose an additional suboptimal solution that leverages a more efficient initial solution to ensure that the resulting solution does not suffer from an unacceptably large information rate loss. We demonstrate that our proposed suboptimal solution is capable of efficiently minimizing disruptions in the event of user population changes by ensuring that the resulting solution experiences minimal, if any, optimization procedures. We also show that our proposed solution, along with the more efficient suboptimal solution introduced in this study, outperforms a more traditional approach that does not account for the base station's overall transmission rate. The results of our study may motivate future research in this area to become a more active area of study in the future. The high complexity of these systems, comprising various components of varying scale and with multiple operational modes, hinders the application of conventional analytical energy estimation techniques. This paper introduces AE-Acc, a computational approach tailored to estimate the energy consumed by accelerators in the context of DNN processing. AE-Acc incorporates two key algorithms. The second, separated from the first, is a recurrent neural network trained on data records of the integrated multi-accellerator architecture, trained against total system energy consumption data in DNN examples, thereby enabling long-term energy consumption forecasting. The effectiveness of AE-Acc is supported by its 3.26% average inaccuracy when predicting the energy consumption of 121 multi-accellerator examples, as well as its 0.63% inaccuracy for 8 out of 121 examples weighing around 10% of their total average energy consumption. an urban area is crucial in managing complex transportation systems, as the local connectivity directly influences traffic flow. This consideration is even more pressing in the context of autonomous vehicles, which will soon be integrated into our road systems. Investigating the topological characteristics of urban street networks is essential to informing policy decisions regarding the deployment of autonomous vehicles and ensuring a smooth transition into a self-driving environment. This study examines the network structure of an urban street system using real-world data from Greater Columbus, Ohio. By employing various topological metrics, we identified clusters of street segments with unique connectivity characteristics. Autonomously driven vehicles could potentially be initially introduced on these isolated network subsets, which were determined to be optimizing traffic flow via a node centrality analysis. Three specific street segments were selected for testing autonomous vehicle deployment, which were found to possess distinct connectivity properties compared to the broader network. Conversely, areas with elevated traffic density and pedestrian activity were found to support a diverse array of street connections, suggesting a more complex relationship between vehicle flow and urban network topology. Ultimately, this study's findings will be used to develop strategies for deploying autonomous vehicles in a way that maximizes traffic efficiency and safety. The research data and code are available at https://github.com/JayJayBao/Urban-Uber-NTF-Analysis. Hartmann initially explored the connection between traffic flow and urban network topology, developing real-world data collection code and demonstrating the importance of selecting test sites based on unique characteristics to isolate autonomous vehicle testing grounds. Jay Jay Bao, who led the research analysis, discovered the correlation between traffic density and connectivity in urban networks, providing valuable insights for autonomous vehicle deployment. developed across various platforms to aid in COVID-19 containment, with some utilizing Bluetooth low energy (BLE) to detect recent infections and others employing camera-based technology to track user movements. As these technologies become increasingly prevalent, they pose critical security and privacy concerns that must be addressed to streamline the global response to the pandemic. In our study, we subject contact tracing apps to a comprehensive evaluation of their data handling and security protocols, focusing on key aspects such as data protection, security, and transparency. Our investigation encompasses a range of measures to assess each app's compliance with data protection legislation, such as the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), and its commitment to operational security and transparency. Upon examining a selection of 32 contact tracing apps, we identify both positive and concerning trends in the implementation of these protocols, with notable shortcomings observed across the board. In contrast to BLE-based apps, those leveraging camera-based technology appear to prioritize user privacy at the expense of functionality, with many employing deceptive tactics to justify the collection and transmission of user location data. In an effort to enhance the security and efficacy of contact tracing initiatives, we provide tailored recommendations to national governments and the organizations operating these systems. Ultimately, our results paint a complex picture of contact tracing apps, with notable strengths and weaknesses that must be carefully balanced in the ongoing battle against COVID-19. In the absence of uniform global data protection legislation and regulatory oversight, the burden of protecting user data ultimately falls on the organizations developing these apps and the users choosing to utilize them. Our research and resulting ratings serve as a resource to inform users on a safer and more efficient contact tracing approach that prioritizes data protection and transparency. In a second phase of our study, we evaluate the performance of 12 COVID-19 contact tracing apps in terms of mass notification capabilities, user engagement, and overall user experience. Our evaluation reveals that a key factor contributing to the success of these apps is their commitment to transparency in data collection, processing, and transmission. In an effort to promote this commitment, we have developed the DECODE award - a prestigious recognition presented to contact tracing apps demonstrating transparency, user understanding, and data protection. Our study has shown that contact tracing apps can effectively rely on end-users for support in COVID-19 mitigation efforts. In the final stage of our research, we have designed a brand-new contact tracing app, DECODE CT, equipped with innovative features that safeguard user data, streamline user awareness of location tracking, and provide an optimal user experience. Despite its numerous achievements, it is often hindered by the complexity of designing algorithms and crafting precise data representations to accurately interpret the solution. To overcome this limitation, the concept of genetic programming was developed to minimize manual programming involvement, thus enabling it to automatically craft both the control structures and data representations needed to tackle a given problem. Although genetic programming was initially envisioned to eliminate the need for human intervention, it ultimately relies on problem-encoded initial genomes, which require expert configuration, as well as function and terminal sets, which are also guided by expert knowledge to achieve optimal performance. Furthermore, genetic programming was initially intended to produce compact, parsimonious solutions, which are difficult to develop manually due to their intricate nature. However, these beneficial traits come at the cost of a relatively small set of available options, which hinders the overall automation of the programming process. To address this limitation, we propose a novel, highly automated approach to programming in the form of genetic road-building in traffic, which is known for its inherently complex algorithms and demanding data requirements. Our study demonstrates that by combining multiple automated programming components, we can achieve significant, multi-faceted improvements in genetic programming outcomes for a variety of complex problems, even with limited genome complexity. Our findings also emphasize the value of jointly exploring the space of genetic parameters and function and terminal sets to uncover innovative solutions, as well as the potential of genetic road-building as a valuable testing ground for assessing and refining automated programming approaches. Upon exciting the junction with a multi-femtosecond pulse, separated from the main laser beam by a demagnifying lens, we observe two phenomena. Firstly, in certain material combinations and under optimal conditions, the relative timing of the exciton formation and disassociation can be precisely manipulated, creating an ultrafast spectral modulation. Secondly, due to the superposition of the excitons with the unstimulated part of the junction, an accelerated exciton population grows extremely quickly, leading to the generation of excitons through intravalley scattering within one cycle of the laser. This outcome is supported by extensive 1D and 2D numerical simulations modelling the interaction of the excitation with the valence band over multiple oscillations. Importantly, we demonstrate the capability to control both the exciton population and the synchronized emission using the timeline of the laser pulse, its intensity and its phase. The observed behavior is specifically applicable to 2D semiconductors and can offer a fresh approach to understanding and managing exciton dynamics in these materials. However, the underlying principles can be applied, with some modifications, to a wide range of materials and systems featuring strongly correlated valence bands. As a result, we propose a pioneering technique to investigate the intrinsic characteristics of valence bands and give the normal dynamics of the junction backseat priority, effectively converting a 2D system into a coherent, efficient, and controllable generator of valence-to-conduction band transitions. The unique feature of our approach lies in its ability to generate minuscule amounts of valence-to-conduction band transitions concentrated in an extremely narrow phase interval lasting only one oscillation. Furthermore, we suggest a range of exciting and innovative applications for the proposed setup, encompassing systems with and without symmetry, Strontium Tantalate coupled with EMIT materials, superconductors and finally, the possibility of harnessing the emitted electrons to create high-energy harmonics, leveraging the single-cycle control over the excitations. The potential implications of this work extend beyond the realm of exciton control, opening the door to valence band manipulation. The novel concept of our study can be summarized as an ultrafast, coherent valve regulating the flow of electrons from the valence band to the conduction band, enabled through the innovative application of laser pulse demagnification, exciton generation and punctual electron emission, uncovering a fresh pathway

In order to improve graph neural networks for node classification on highly clustered graphs, we introduce Disserp, a novel framework that utilizes sparse projection methods to enhance representation learning.  Disserp distinguables itself from existing methods by employing a novel sparse projection operator, incorporating in its linear combinations only the neighbourhood of immediate and direct neighbours of a given node, thereby effectively handling graph structures with high clustering.  The effectiveness of our approach is substantiated by setting up a new theoretical framework that provides explicit bounds for Disserp's performance and validating these bounds through experiments.  The results show that Disserp consistently outperforms current state-of-the-art methods for node classification and is successfully applied to a variety of real-world datasets, including those with extremely dense clusters.  The code used in our research is made freely available.  The name 'Disserp' is derived from the German word for "disjoint" and the 'p' suffix signifies projection, highlighting the role of disjoint neighbourhoods in our approach.  The project can be accessed at https://github.com/leoprec/Disserp.  The paper at its core explores the question of how graph structural characteristics influence the development of effective node classification methods for graph neural networks.  The 'disjoint' in Disserp refers to the fact that the neighbourhoods of the linear combinations are always disjoint, which in turn reduces clustering-related difficulties in graph neural networks.  The 'p' in Disserp represents the projection operator, emphasizing the importance of sparse projection in our approach.  The value of incorporating neighbourhoods from the immediate and direct neighbours of a given node lies in the enhanced gradient norms and the resulting improved node classification.  The theoretical framework set up in our research is novel and involves the use of operator norms to provide bounds for Disserp's performance. By conducting large-scale experimental observations, researchers have noticed the formation of coal particles into various-size groups in the furnace, a phenomenon that has not previously been simulated.  This study aims to examine the effect of sizing coal particles by type on combustion behavior in the furnace's upper section using computer simulations to inform possible modifications to furnace design.  To begin, we ran computer simulations of furnace combustion using different-sized coal particles, evenly distributed in diameter from 40 to 250 micrometers, to establish a reference point for subsequent experiments.  To make our simulations align with experimental observations in the furnace's upper section, we applied a non-uniform distribution of coal particles in terms of size and position in the furnace to model a region near the furnace's upper section.  This unique coal particle distribution allowed for the simulation of two phenomena observed during experimental observations in the furnace's upper section: the formation of large 'coal particles of various-size groups' and the formation of pulverized coal into streams or streams.  Our results show that sizing coal particles by type on-scales impacts the rate at which coal particles burn in the furnace's upper section, a rate that can be optimized for a more efficient furnace design.  This study highlights the importance of considering the sizing of coal particles by type when simulating, designing, and executing experiments on furnace combustion, a phenomenon.  This study shows that sizing coal particles by type allows for the efficient combustion of coal particles in the furnace's upper section.  Results indicate that burning coal particles reach temperatures as high as 1700 K in the furnace's upper section when sized by type, a temperature that reflects the average temperature of a furnace's cross-section.  If coal particles are uniformly sized at 40 to 250 micrometers, the temperature of combustion is reduced by as much as 300 K, a phenomenon that serves as the basis for understanding the effect of sizing coal particles by type on combustion in the furnace's upper section. In this research, we focus on detecting and distilling learning representations that have notably distinct characteristics, by utilizing a measure of categorical separation within the Repertory Grid Formalism. This notion was initially introduced by Kelly in 1955 and is defined as the difference in the standard deviations of two learning representations, typically ranging from 1 to 10. We have identified three scenarios where this separation measure is particularly useful: (i) exploring representations with substantial differences; (ii) detecting bias in models due to varying attributes; and (iii) extracting and visualizing distinct concepts from a single model. To achieve these goals, we developed a Distinct Learning Representation Generator (DLRG) that utilizes self-supervised learning, as well as an associated metric to identify and refine the desired representations. Moreover, our analysis demonstrates that the proposed approach can be effectively applied to the aforementioned scenarios. The methodology will be made available upon request, and the required code can be accessed at this GitHub repository, https://github.com/ramyaresearch/DLRG. We have applied our DLRG method in multiple settings, namely, (i) a qualitative study of medical images developed by Gillette et al. in 2019 to explore their intrinsic properties; (ii) an analysis of English autocephalous churches to detect their distinct characteristics; (iii) a demonstration of how a pre-trained Spacy model for English language has been influenced by biases in topics such as gender, race, and sexuality; (iv) an application of our DLRG method in conjunction with a pre-trained ImageNet model, revealing that it can capture notable concepts within the network; (v) an application of our DLRG method in conjunction with a neural network trained on BoB, a late intermediate level BBC dataset. We have also conducted an empirical study to verify that the Repertory Grid Formalism's separation measure (greater than 1) is effective for categorizing objects, as opposed to using the Euclidean distance metric (greater than 1) or any value within that range. Introduced by Kelly in 1955, the Repertory Grid Formalism, also known as the grid technique, is a method used for conceptually understanding human perception and learning representations. According to simulations, the absorbed energy by these polyurethane microspheres can store substantial energy (approximately 80 J/m) and produce significant frictional resistance (~ 80 MPa) due to their intense mechanical bonding with the matrix, leading to increased fracture toughness. Experimental findings and numerical calculations revealed that polyurethane microspheres completely soaked in the matrix significantly reduced their inherent mechanical weaknesses, resulting in substantial toughness enhancements. This research can serve as a reference for enhancing the fracture toughness of nanocomposites and microspheres in general. As an added advantage, tailoring the microspheres and interfacial bond strength offers the potential for extensive toughness variations. Overall, our findings show the immense potential for improving the fracture toughness of microspheres by strengthening their interfacial connection with the surrounding matrix. In contrast, loosely attached microspheres failed to boost toughness due to their inability to effectively dissipate energy through crack deviation. Nonetheless, our study pinpoints that optimizing the microspheres' complete immersion in the matrix, facilitated by intense interfacial bonding, as the pivotal factor for maximizing toughness through efficient crack diversion and surface stabilization mechanisms. Developing a suitable feature engineering approach for channel statistics to guide CSI normalization and facilitate deep learning is an underdeveloped area. Inspired by the channel response characteristics observed in existing 2D imaging applications, we introduce a U-shaped feature engineering approach for channel statistics to normalize CSI for deep learning in localization. Specifically, we generate a U-shaped feature map by combining spatial channel response patterns in the spatial and temporal dimensions with the support vector machine classification of CSI. The classified CSI is then utilized for normalization, and the resulting normalized CSI exhibits consistent location-related features throughout the data collection. Consequently, a deep learning model can successfully generalize from limited data. Our array represents a generalized version of the Kronecker graph, and our study shows that the convergence rate for these systems arrays dimensionality equals the square of the number of bundles. Considerable research has been done on this topic, with results indicating that the success of deep networks heavily relies on their application. The present study focuses on using Neural Networks as trial functions in quantum Monte Carlo methods and discovers that a specific architecture is equally effective whether you're a quantum expert or not. The simple architecture involves using the same network for both potential and Hamiltonian calculations, whereas more complex architectures involve employing distinct networks for these purposes. To determine the optimal network complexity, non-deep methods were previously reliant on the number of basis states or points, but this study shows that the same rule applies even with more advanced architectures. The ultimate success of a quantum neural network also depends on optimizing its parameters, a process made easier with the use of more advanced methods such as stochastic gradient descent. The above findings were tested using various quantum equations including the hydrogen atom, he-likin, and ho-likin systems, proving successful. The approaches explored in the present study are, to our knowledge, the first time these complex systems have been solved using Neural Networks as trial functions. The understanding gained on the choice of network architecture is, therefore, an important advancement for the novel quantum applications in areas such as chemistry and physics. The present study also sheds light on its own algorithms, revealing, for example, that the speed up of deep networks is mostly due to a significant increase in the signal-to-noise ratio in regions where basins of attraction exist. The discovery of a specific architecture-temperature relationship for complex systems also indicates that the simple architectures used here may not be sufficient at extremely high temperatures. The approaches explored in the present study are available at https://github.com/LucasMoraes9/QNCCuboid. The approaches explored in the present study have the potential to be extended to more complex problems such as quantum field theory, where the choice of network architecture is still completely unknown. In general, to evaluate the impact of a particular condition, an average treatment effect evaluated across multiple trials with varied participant profiles is an approximation, as it assumes uniform applicability.  In reality, though, it's clear that environmental factors influence the outcome of treatments, leading researchers to incorporate relevant covariates in an effort to accurately assess the condition's impact.  Unfortunately, the presence of ancillary variables does not necessarily resolve the issue of generalizing treatment effects, as the presence of confounding factors only justifies casual inference but not statistical one.  To efficiently assess the causal adequacy of data from multiple trials, we've devised a new method that uses time an effort, reducing dependence on complex statistical calculations, making it suitable for automated use in trials with numerous variables.  Our approach also allows the rapid identification and valuation of included variables, enabling prioritization of those that significantly impact the causal effect, thus improving the overall efficacy of data combination.  The proposed method has been successfully tested on both simulated and real trial data, with results that reflect the anticipated outcomes, prompting us to recommend its use in trials that aim to establish a general causal effect by combining results from multiple trials.  The associated study can be found at doi:10.1038/s41425-021-00491-7.  The developed method is available through an R package called comboate, which can be downloaded at this link:  https://github.com/cominate/comboate. cosmic ray data covers a remarkable energy range from 10^6 to 10^18 eV, yet still can't address all aspects of the two-source model of their origins. Historically, the two-source model consisted of two unknown components - the single source forming protons and the source of nuclei, but recent data on light and insistent difficulties with the "iron curve" lead researchers to reconsider which source is which. In this paper, we suggest a revised version of the two-source model that incorporates recent data on gamma-ray bursts. We show that primordial nuclei produced by a single source (likely supernovae) cannot be accelerated to energies above 10^15 eV due to fragmentation, but when in space, the nuclei can form large grains (with masses up to 10^5 u) that can survive extreme acceleration, thereby explaining observations up to 10^18 eV and the "iron curve" observed. In contrast, the traditional model fails to achieve this goal. In line with this hypothesis, we predict that future research should uncover GBF with energies up to 10^20 eV, while supernovae should be detectable through the observation of multiple Z elements within a narrow energy range, near 10^16 eV. In addition, the large galactic source should also produce a distinct neutrino signature consisting of multiple muons observed near the Earth, specifically, 12 neutrino events per year involving the muon decay from the interaction of a 100 GeV neutrino with an iron nucleus, and can be experimentally verified by the muon spectroscopy of the Fermi Deep Liquid Scintillator detector. In many organisms, adjacent genes often share related functions, making it essential to analyze their functional linkages to interpret coordinated responses to variable stimuli. As a quantitative approach, we use inter-genic functional associations to measure the connectedness of adjacent gene functions within diverse species, including mouse, rat, and fly. Furthermore, we extended this concept to analyze distant genes through multiple levels of regulatory networks, effectively mapping functional relationships across the entire genome. Notably, our findings display significant persistence of functional connections spanning from primary to secondary locations. Consequently, we propose a two-tiered model to explain coordinated gene responses: the primary tier involves immediate neighbors with direct functional ties, whereas the secondary tier encompasses more distant genes with similar functions, whose responses are derivatively stimulated. In contrast, random arrangements of genes lack persistent functional connections, as evidenced by our analysis under neutral conditions. Overall, our study highlights the prominent role of localized genetic functions and their extended functional networks in determining coordinated gene responses across diverse organisms. As an integrated strategy to control the mite's infestation, essential oil-based treatments are being widely adopted. However, the key challenge lies in determining the optimal combination of essential oils that can effectively eliminate the varroa mite infestation while safeguarding the honeybee colony. A comprehensive analysis is presented to find the ideal combination of clove, thyme, and lemongrass essential oils that can successfully control varroa mite infestations. recognizing human actions efficiently is essential, but current algorithms 
don't meet this requirement due to increasing complexity as more data is used.
A more practical approach would be a system that can learn and recognize actions
using low storage and computational costs by utilizing compact models.
To address this need, a novel network architecture, called Fischer Action Detector (FAD),
has been proposed. Inspired by the concept of kernel method using differentiable 
kernels from the Fischer et al. paper, the FAD is an end-to-end, deep neural 
network designed for efficient learning and recognition of actions.
To implement this concept in a deep neural network, the Gaussian Mixture Model 
(GMM) was chosen as a reference, and the network was optimized to reproduce 
GMM's characteristics using differentiable kernels' gradients.
As a result, the FAD offers end-to-end visual appearance and motion information
for effective action recognition, while its compact storage size allows the model
to operate with reduced memory at a lower cost and computational complexity compared
to traditional CNNs, as evidenced by its UPEV and AVEY dataset results. 
The source code for the Fischer Action Detector has been made available at (https://github.com/indigo-mL/FAD). 
The FAD's distinguished feature is its low storage requirements, as it outperforms 
traditional CNNs in terms of memory efficiency by a factor of 12 and the previous 
best model, C-DNN-BM, by a factor of 2.6. 
Additionally, the FAD's computational complexity is less than traditional CNNs 
by a factor of 2 and the previous best model, C-DNN-Bm, by a factor of 1.4. 
The FAD's weight vector across all three layers sums to approximately 18k, 
as compared to C-DNN-Bm's 48k, and traditional CNNs' 104k.

is minimal at around 1%, as documented in the paper.

memory and computational efficiency improvements over previous models.

such as employing more complex kernels, increasing video frames, and incorporating audio information.

data in fast magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) requires an inverse Fourier transform.  To make the most of limited data, we use the Laplacian heuristic to enhance the available k-space information.  This approach can be seen as adding zero-filling dimensions to partially reconstruct k-space data.  A key challenge is choosing the optimal number of dimensions, which we resolve by utilizing the structured low-rank bandit minimizer with a regularization term.  Our proposed method, the bandit under-sampling algorithm (BUA), successfully reconstructs k-space data from a limited number of measurements.  Specifically, we evaluated BUA in relation to several established algorithms -- direct inverse, iterative low-rank assignment, both direct inverse with local low-rank regularization and direct inverse with non-local low-rank regularization -- using synthetic and real-world data.  Our results from these experiments show that BUA, along with the non-local low-rank regularization method, yield the most accurate reconstructions when applied to the Laplacian heuristic.  Additionally, we found that BUA generally outperforms the iterative low-rank assignment algorithm in terms of reconstruction quality and compression rate.  Our algorithm has also been successfully applied to real-world data, yielding high-quality reconstructions from highly compressed k-space data.  A source code implementation of BUA is available on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/Harsha-Faruq/BUA.  Our proposed algorithm, BUA, is easily implementable and serves as an efficient solution for reconstructing data sampled at high speeds in MRI.  It outperforms comparable algorithms in terms of compression and reconstruction quality and can be used in various forms of linear inverse problems involving high-speed sampling.  Our algorithm has also been adapted and applied to video de-blurring, demonstrating efficient reconstruction results with high quality images.  We observed the non-local and temporal relationship among video frames, enabling the successful removal of video blurriness.  Our algorithm is based on the structured low-rank bandit minimizer with a regularization term and is easily implementable.  It outperforms the iterative shrinkage thresholding algorithm in terms of compression and reconstruction quality and can be used in various forms of linear inverse problems involving high-speed sampling.  Our algorithm, BUA, is an under-active exploration method that successfully reconstructs data from a limited number of measurements. Decision-making processes often involve comparing two graphs, either directly or by identifying one that meets specific criteria. The problem of determining whether a graph meets specified quantitative requirements is well-established, with the parameterized version being well-studied on general graphs. However, the situation is more complicated with weighted graphs, so we propose a limited set of graph properties applicable to weighted graphs and focus on their parameterized complexity. The properties we examine are related to graph diameter, specifically looking for patterns that require a limited number of edges to connect two vertices or those within a specific bound. These properties also extend to identifying patterns that must exist within weighted graphs, as well as those that, on average, exhibit certain weight distributions. The goal is to offer a framework that allows us to accurately compare two weighted graphs, first by identifying one that minimally meets specific requirements, and then by finding the graph that most closely meets these specifications. The results we obtain are largely positive, with the exception of finding patterns with limited diameters, a problem we demonstrate to be equivalent to the Longest Shortest Path problem, a problem that has been proven to be highly parameterized. performance of modern neural network predictors, known as "black boxes," is a primary focus in the field of postdictive analysis. Recently, research has been conducted to examine the source of generalization using supervised learning frameworks, however there has been minimal examination of the unsupervised learning paradigm. This study demonstrates that generalization in the unsupervised setting of out-of-distribution (OoD) detection is influenced by two distinct components, one governed by Bayesian principles and the other by entropy-based principles. By decoupling these components, it is possible to accurately predict the unsupervised generalization performance of complex deep neural network models, simply through examination of their behavior on easily generated synthetic data. Moreover, these models can also be applied to various challenging OoD datasets,affording significantly smaller dataset sizes for evaluation. system of interacting elements is analyzed through the casting process, where the connections between components are represented as distinct entities. The casting process involves mapping the interactions between nodes in a network to a new landscape with nodes representing bonds and new edges indicating the relationships between these bonds. The casting of various networks - including star, clique, complete, and random networks - is investigated along with the inverse process of reversing the relationships between their constituent parts. The study reveals that the casting process preserves key properties of a network and allows for a more nuanced understanding of its structure. It demonstrates that in networks where the relationships between nodes are unique, a new network can be generated through the casting process with improved modularity; this is shown in random networks and in the network representing the interactions between athletes in the NBA. The study also shows the casting process can effectively represent the topology of a network including the relationships between its constituent parts as well as the relationships between its distinct entities.
